title: How to Seed Reviews for a New Product Launch
excerpt: A launch with zero reviews converts worse than the same product with ten honest ones. Here is how to seed early reviews without buying them, breaking platform rules, or annoying your first customers.
body: A product page with no reviews forces the shopper to do all the risk assessment alone. Ten honest reviews, even mixed ones, usually outperform a perfect but empty page, because they answer the questions a description cannot: does it fit, does it feel cheap, does it arrive on time. Seeding those first reviews is a launch task rather than an afterthought. The Reviews category at /category/reviews keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing for review platforms.

Start before launch with a small, clearly labeled group. Send the product to a few dozen existing customers, email subscribers, or community members at no cost and tell them plainly that you would value an honest review, including a critical one. Do not offer payment for a positive review, and do not ask for five stars. Rewarding honest feedback is acceptable in most markets; conditioning a reward on a positive rating is not, and it creates exactly the legal and platform risk you are trying to avoid.

Time the request to the moment the product has been used. Reviews written the day a box arrives describe shipping rather than the product, and that is a wasted slot on your page. For consumables, wait two or three weeks. For apparel, wait until after the first wash. For anything with a learning curve, wait long enough that the customer has actually figured it out. A simple rule works well: trigger the request as the return window is about to close instead of the morning after delivery.

Ask better questions than a blank box. An open form produces one word answers. Prompts produce usable copy: what problem were you trying to solve, what nearly stopped you from buying, how did sizing or setup go. Those answers give you review text written in the language real shoppers search with, and they double as product page copy and ad angles. Keep the form short, because completion falls off sharply once you add a third required field.

Make the mechanics frictionless. One email, one tap, no login. If your review platform requires an account to submit, expect most people to abandon halfway. Photo and video requests should be a separate optional step with an obvious example, because showing what a good submission looks like roughly doubles the media rate. Reply to the first wave publicly, especially the critical ones, since visible replies signal that a real business is reading and fixing things.

Then keep the tap open permanently. Seeding solves launch week; a request flow attached to every fulfilled order solves month six. Route reviews onto the product page, surface them on collection pages and in email, and watch whether reviews per order drift down over time, which usually means the request email has stopped landing. You can compare request flows, media collection, and pricing on the Okendo page at /tool/okendo, and see other review platforms in the Reviews category at /category/reviews.
